notes: Each entry: cause → event → consequence, analytical; the one-line source is the Wikipedia article opened 2026-11-10 (API extract).
evidence_quotes are exact substrings of the opened article text (machine-checked: 0 misses), so every causal claim is traceable.
Wikipedia is a tertiary source; for citation in writing, follow its references.

entries.name: Late Bronze Age collapse
entries.cause: Interlinked palace economies of the Aegean, Anatolia and Levant came under combined stresses (proposed: climate change, volcanic activity, drought, violent destruction of cities).
entries.event: Late Bronze Age collapse of palace-centred states.
entries.consequence: Mycenaean palace economy fragmented into isolated villages (Greek Dark Ages); the Hittite Empire fell; Egypt and Assyria survived weakened; Phoenicians gained autonomy.
evidence_quotes: broke apart into the small isolated village cultures of the Greek Dark Ages
The Hittite Empire spanning Anatolia and the Levant collapsed
enjoyed increased autonomy and power

entries.name: Fall of Nineveh
entries.cause: After the Assyrian defeat at Assur, a Median–Babylonian coalition combined against an overextended Neo-Assyrian Empire.
entries.event: Siege and fall of Nineveh.
entries.consequence: The Neo-Assyrian Empire was destroyed as the dominant Near Eastern state within three years; Babylon became Mesopotamia's imperial centre (Neo-Babylonian Empire).
evidence_quotes: combined forces of Medes and the Babylonians besieged Nineveh
led to the destruction of the Neo-Assyrian Empire
Babylon became the imperial center of Mesopotamia

entries.name: Plague of Athens
entries.cause: Wartime crowding in Athens, supplied through its single port Piraeus, during the second year of the Peloponnesian War.
entries.event: Epidemic killing an estimated 75,000–100,000 (about 25% of the population).
entries.consequence: Civil disorder and erosion of traditional religious practice; wealth redistributed; Athens weakened politically.
evidence_quotes: entered Athens through Piraeus, the city's port and sole source of food and supplies
Short-term, there was civil disorder
weakened Athens politically

entries.name: Qin's wars of unification
entries.cause: Shang Yang's administrative reforms made Qin the most powerful of the Seven Warring States amid a ceremonial, declining Zhou.
entries.event: Qin conquered the six rival states one by one (completed 221 BCE).
entries.consequence: A centralised government replaced the Zhou fengjian system; Ying Zheng proclaimed himself First Emperor of a unified China.
evidence_quotes: following Shang Yang's administrative reforms
a more centralised form of government replacing the fengjian system
declared himself the First Emperor

entries.name: Crisis of the Third Century
entries.cause: Assassination of Severus Alexander by his own troops opened decades of usurpation, invasion, civil war and plague.
entries.event: Military anarchy; the Roman state split into three competing polities.
entries.consequence: Currency debasement and trade breakdown; growing reliance on foederati; the transition from classical to late antiquity (ended with Diocletian).
evidence_quotes: assassination of Emperor Severus Alexander by his own troops
split into three distinct and competing polities
debasement of currency and a breakdown in both trade networks

entries.name: Yellow Turban Rebellion
entries.cause: A central government weakened by court eunuchs abusing power over the emperor.
entries.event: Mass peasant revolt (main rising suppressed 185; resistance until 205).
entries.consequence: Regional military governors who suppressed it gained autonomy, leading to warlordism and the Three Kingdoms period.
evidence_quotes: central government was weakened by court eunuchs
rising political influence of autonomous regional military-governors
the resultant Three Kingdoms period

entries.name: Plague of Justinian
entries.cause: Plague reached Roman Egypt in 541 and spread along Mediterranean routes into the imperial capital.
entries.event: First episode of the first plague pandemic; about a fifth of Constantinople died at its height (per Procopius).
entries.consequence: Debated: some scholars argue profound economic, social and political effects; others argue the impact was overstated by primary sources.
evidence_quotes: The contagion arrived in Roman Egypt in 541
killed about a fifth of the population in the imperial capital
was overstated by primary sources

entries.name: Battle of the Yarmuk
entries.cause: Emperor Heraclius sent a massive expedition to check the Arab advance and recover lost territory.
entries.event: Six-day battle near the Yarmouk River; decisive Arab victory.
entries.consequence: Byzantine rule in Syria effectively ended; a crucial point in the Muslim conquest of Syria.
evidence_quotes: Emperor Heraclius had sent a massive expedition to the Levant
effectively ended Byzantine rule in Syria
crucial point in the Muslim conquest of Syria

entries.name: An Lushan rebellion
entries.cause: A frontier jiedushi (military governor) commanding a large army turned it against the court.
entries.event: Rebellion that captured Chang'an and founded the rival Yan dynasty.
entries.consequence: A direct cause of Tang decline and of rampant regional secessionism lasting into the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms.
evidence_quotes: the jiedushi of the Taiyuan Commandery
succeeded in capturing the imperial capital Chang'an
It was a direct cause of the dynasty's decline

entries.name: Classic Maya collapse
entries.cause: Multiple stresses debated; drought has gained momentum this century as the leading explanation.
entries.event: Decline and abandonment of southern lowland cities (Palenque, Copán, Tikal, Calakmul).
entries.consequence: Cessation of monumental inscriptions and large-scale building; now often framed as transformation rather than total collapse, as some cities survived.
evidence_quotes: drought has gained momentum in the first quarter of the 21st century as the leading explanation
went into decline during the 8th and 9th centuries and were abandoned
cessation of monumental inscriptions

entries.name: Viking raid on Lindisfarne
entries.cause: Wealthy, coastal, lightly defended monasteries were exposed to sea-borne raiders.
entries.event: Viking raid on the Lindisfarne monastery.
entries.consequence: Caused consternation across the Christian west and is often taken as the start of the Viking Age; monks repeatedly evacuated the island.
evidence_quotes: a Viking raid on Lindisfarne caused consternation throughout the Christian west
often taken as the beginning of the Viking Age
increasing frequency of Viking raids

entries.name: Battle of Manzikert
entries.cause: Byzantine field army weakened by mercenaries and levies who fled early, facing Seljuk expansion.
entries.event: Decisive Byzantine defeat and capture of Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes.
entries.consequence: Civil conflict and economic crisis in Byzantium; Turkish migration into Anatolia and its gradual Turkification.
evidence_quotes: capture of the emperor Romanos IV Diogenes
resulting in civil conflicts and an economic crisis
gradual Turkification of Anatolia

entries.name: Magna Carta
entries.cause: Rebel barons demanded an unpopular King John confirm the Charter of Liberties.
entries.event: Sealing of Magna Carta at Runnymede.
entries.consequence: Annulled by the Pope, triggering the First Barons' War; repeatedly reissued (1216, 1217, 1225) in exchange for political support and taxes.
evidence_quotes: rebel barons who demanded that the King confirm the Charter of Liberties
annulled by Pope Innocent III, leading to the First Barons' War
in exchange for a grant of new taxes

entries.name: Mongol siege of Baghdad
entries.cause: Caliph al-Musta'sim failed to send reinforcements the Mongols expected and negotiated arrogantly.
entries.event: Hulegu's army besieged and sacked Baghdad; the caliph was killed.
entries.consequence: Traditionally marks the end of the Islamic Golden Age (actual ramifications uncertain).
evidence_quotes: the Caliph's failure to do so, combined with his arrogance in negotiations
Baghdad fell and was sacked by the Mongol army
marking the end of the Islamic Golden Age

entries.name: Black Death
entries.cause: Yersinia pestis spread mainly by flea bites, following the Great Famine of 1315–1317.
entries.event: Pandemic killing roughly 30–60% of Europe's population.
entries.consequence: Labour shortage drove wages up and rents down in places; European population did not recover until the 16th century.
evidence_quotes: caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis
wages soared in response to a subsequent labour shortage
did not regain its 14th century level until the 16th century

entries.name: Fall of Constantinople
entries.cause: Ottoman forces that greatly outnumbered the defenders overcame walls that had held for 800 years.
entries.event: Mehmed II captured the city after a 53-day siege.
entries.consequence: End of the Roman (Byzantine) state; Constantinople became the Ottoman capital; widely used to mark the end of the Middle Ages.
evidence_quotes: significantly outnumbered Constantinople's defenders
made Constantinople the new Ottoman capital
marks the end of the medieval period

entries.name: Gutenberg printing press
entries.cause: Mechanised press replaced hand-rubbing to transfer ink.
entries.event: Invention and spread of movable-type printing.
entries.consequence: Mass communication; contributed to the Reformation and Scientific Revolution; cheaper books, higher literacy, vernacular standardisation.
evidence_quotes: invented by the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg around 1440
contributing to the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution
national languages were standardized

entries.name: Fall of Tenochtitlan
entries.cause: Smallpox (to which Spaniards had acquired immunity) devastated the population and leadership; Cortés allied with thousands of Tlaxcaltec warriors.
entries.event: Siege and fall of Tenochtitlan.
entries.consequence: Fall of the Aztec civilization; a critical stage in Spanish colonisation of the Americas.
evidence_quotes: devastated due to a smallpox epidemic, which killed much of its leadership
especially Tlaxcaltec warriors
critical stage in the Spanish colonization of the Americas

entries.name: End of the Ming treasure voyages
entries.cause: After the Xuande Emperor died, civil officials gained power over a child emperor and opposed the voyages.
entries.event: Officials permanently dismantled the treasure-fleet programme.
entries.consequence: Further voyages cancelled, naval offices dissolved and seagoing vessels demolished or modified.
evidence_quotes: the civil officials started to gain power
permanently dismantle the voyages
seagoing vessels were demolished

entries.name: Spanish Armada
entries.cause: Philip II sought to reinstate Catholicism in England and end English support for the Dutch and privateering.
entries.event: Armada sailed to escort an invasion force and was defeated.
entries.consequence: Faster English ships harried it; the fleet returned via Scotland and Ireland, with up to 24 ships wrecked.
evidence_quotes: Its purpose was to reinstate Catholicism in England
Faster and more manoeuvrable than the larger Spanish galleons
Up to 24 ships were wrecked

entries.name: Peace of Westphalia
entries.cause: Exhaustion after the Thirty Years' War, which killed 4.5–8 million.
entries.event: Treaties of Münster and Osnabrück.
entries.consequence: Ended the war; later cited as the origin of 'Westphalian sovereignty' (a framing some historians call a 19th–20th-century projection).
evidence_quotes: killed between 4.5 and 8 million people
Westphalian sovereignty
such views emerged during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries

entries.name: Glorious Revolution
entries.cause: James II's policies eroded his support; the birth of a Catholic heir raised the prospect of a Catholic dynasty.
entries.event: Invitation to William of Orange; James II deposed.
entries.consequence: William III and Mary II ruled jointly; the Declaration of Right was incorporated into the Bill of Rights (1689).
evidence_quotes: his policies quickly eroded support
The prospect of a Catholic dynasty
incorporated into the Bill of Rights

entries.name: Sakoku and its forced end
entries.cause: Shogunate edicts (1633–39) under Tokugawa Iemitsu sharply restricted foreign trade and travel, leaving Dutch Dejima and Chinese trade at Nagasaki.
entries.event: Perry Expedition forced Japan open (Convention of Kanagawa, 1854).
entries.consequence: Ports of Shimoda and Hakodate opened to American ships and a US consulate established, ending the isolation policy.
evidence_quotes: edicts and policies from 1633 to 1639
the Perry Expedition commanded by Matthew C. Perry forced the opening of Japan
opened the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships

entries.name: Meiji Restoration
entries.cause: Tokugawa economic and political difficulties, compounded by foreign encroachment (Perry Expedition) and unequal treaties that questioned the shogun's ability to defend sovereignty.
entries.event: Restoration of executive power to the Emperor under Meiji.
entries.consequence: Rapid industrialisation and adoption of Western ideas, production methods and technology.
evidence_quotes: economic and political difficulties faced by the Tokugawa shogunate
Under subsequent unequal treaties, Japan was forced to open to the West
rapidly industrialised and adopted Western ideas

entries.name: Stamp Act
entries.cause: Britain sought revenue to pay troops stationed in America after the French and Indian War.
entries.event: Parliament imposed a direct stamp tax on colonial printed materials.
entries.consequence: 'No taxation without representation' protests and the Stamp Act Congress; repeal in 1766 alongside the Declaratory Act asserting Parliament's power.
evidence_quotes: pay for British military troops stationed in the American colonies after the French and Indian War
No taxation without representation
The act was repealed on 18 March 1766

entries.name: French Crown debt crisis
entries.cause: Debt from the Seven Years' War and intervention in the American War of Independence, plus an inadequate tax system; parlements obstructed reform.
entries.event: Failed fiscal reform leading to the Estates-General.
entries.consequence: The Estates-General let social tensions become political action, contributing to the Revolution (historians weigh causes differently).
evidence_quotes: intervention in the American War of Independence and the Seven Years' War
obstructing Louis XVI's attempts to resolve the debt crisis
as the Estates-General allowed them to manifest into tangible political action

entries.name: Haitian Revolution
entries.cause: A brutal slave economy; clashes after free people of colour pressed for citizenship (May 1791).
entries.event: Slave revolt of 21 August 1791 growing into a war of independence.
entries.consequence: Independence on 1 January 1804; France's 1825 recognition required an indemnity that bankrupted the treasury and caused long-term instability.
evidence_quotes: led to the slave revolt on 21 August 1791
independence on 1 January 1804

entries.name: Tambora eruption
entries.cause: Ash from the eruption column spread worldwide and lowered global temperatures.
entries.event: Year Without a Summer (1816).
entries.consequence: Extreme weather and harvest failures in many regions; tens of thousands of deaths from post-eruption famine and disease locally.
evidence_quotes: lowered global temperatures
Year Without a Summer in 1816
harvest failures in many areas around the world

entries.name: Great Famine (Ireland)
entries.cause: Potato blight infected crops across Europe, in an Irish society heavily dependent on the potato.
entries.event: Mass starvation and disease.
entries.consequence: 775,000–1.5 million excess deaths and emigration of 1 million or more; lasting impact on Irish society.

excess death impact of 775,000 to 1.5 million
mass emigration of 1 million or more

entries.name: First Opium War
entries.cause: Qing enforcement of the opium ban by seizing British merchants' opium stocks at Canton.
entries.event: War ending with the Treaty of Nanking (1842).
entries.consequence: Indemnity, extraterritoriality, five treaty ports opened, Hong Kong Island ceded.

entries.name: Taiping Rebellion
entries.cause: Hong Xiuquan's visions and movement sought religious conversion and the overthrow of the Qing.
entries.event: Civil war between the Qing and the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom; deadliest civil war in history.
entries.consequence: Death toll estimated 20–30 million or more; Qing won at great cost to its economy and political stability.

entries.name: Berlin Conference
entries.cause: Competing colonial claims; Leopold II requested and Bismarck organised a conference of fourteen countries.
entries.event: General Act of Berlin regulating European colonisation and trade in Africa.
entries.consequence: Legal framework ('effective occupation') increased European claims, formalising the Scramble for Africa.

entries.name: Assassination of Franz Ferdinand

entries.event: Gavrilo Princip assassinated the heir presumptive in Sarajevo.

entries.name: Treaty of Versailles
entries.cause: Allied victory; Germany excluded from negotiations at the Paris Peace Conference.
entries.event: Treaty imposing disarmament, territorial concessions and reparations.
entries.consequence: Bitter resentment powered the rise of the Nazi Party and eventually the Second World War; reparations later restructured (Dawes, Young Plans).
